     “The latent factor of LLM intelligence”. Follows book/LLM-STYLE-GUIDE.md.
     Rows for papers with no archived fulltext (ilic2024positive, kipnis2025metabench,
     maimon2025iq, and everything from late 2025 on) paraphrase rather than quote;
     numbers there come from abstracts and the papers' own text. Written 2026-09. -->

The evidence is a run of psychometric analyses of model-by-benchmark score matrices, starting in mid-2023 with 29 models on HELM and growing to several hundred models on the Open LLM Leaderboard by 2025, plus a newer line of work that builds one-dimensional capability scales by construction (item response theory). Nearly every study finds a positive manifold and a large first factor; they disagree on whether what remains after it is noise or structure, and the answer moves with the sample of models and benchmarks chosen.

| Date | Paper | Setting | Findings | Figure |
|:--|:-----|:----|:--------------|:----------|
| 2023-06 | *Revealing the Structure of Language Model Capabilities*<br>@burnell2023reveal | 29 LLMs (GPT-3 series, OPT, BLOOM, J1, Cohere, TNLG v2; releases 05/2020–03/2023) on 27 HELM tasks | **Task scores form a positive manifold with mean inter-task correlation r = 0.56.**<br>**Exploratory factor analysis prefers three correlated factors, not one.** Reasoning, comprehension and core language modelling explain 33%, 31% and 17% of variance (82% cumulative); inter-factor correlations 0.22–0.51. They find "three clear factors, each of which explains a substantial proportion of the variance".<br>**Model size loads mainly on the first factor.** Log parameter count correlates 0.70, 0.49 and 0.51 with the three factors. | |
| 2024-01 | *How predictable is language model benchmark performance?*<br>@owen2024predictable | BIG-Bench and BBH: 11–18 architectures, 36–44 model sizes, 2M–540B parameters; MMLU incl. GPT-4 | **Aggregate benchmark performance is predicted by a single scalar, scaled compute, across independently trained architectures.** BBH mean absolute error 3.9pp across a doubling of compute; individual BIG-Bench tasks 17pp mean error. "Aggregated benchmarks, averaging over many individual tasks, are much more predictable". No factor analysis. | |
| 2024-02 | *tinyBenchmarks: evaluating LLMs with fewer examples*<br>@polo2024tinybenchmarks | Open LLM Leaderboard benchmarks (MMLU has 14K items) | **One hundred curated items suffice to estimate a model's MMLU score.** Item response theory: the item-by-model matrix is well described by a low-dimensional latent ability. | |
| 2024-05 | *Observational Scaling Laws and the Predictability of Language Model Performance*<br>@ruan2024observational | 77 pretrained base models from 21 families on 8 benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-C, HellaSwag, Winogrande, GSM8K, HumanEval, TruthfulQA, XWinograd); instruction-tuned appendix adds GPT-4 and Claude 2 | **The first principal component explains nearly 80% of the variation and is a weighted average of all benchmarks.** Top 3 PCs ~97% (98.6% for instruction-tuned models).<br>**PC-1 is log-linear in training compute within each model family, with R² > 0.9.** "the LMs’ PC-1 measure linearly correlates with their log-training FLOPs".<br>**The residual components carry signal.** Their method keeps 3 PCs; PC-2 loads on reasoning, PC-3 on programming. | ![Variance explained by the first five PCs across 77 models, from @ruan2024observational](images/image4.png) |
| 2024-07 | *metabench – A Sparse Benchmark of Reasoning and Knowledge in Large Language Models*<br>@kipnis2025metabench | Six Open LLM Leaderboard benchmarks, one IRT model each; ICLR 2025 | **A single common factor tracks total benchmark score almost perfectly.** They report "a single underlying common factor whose Spearman correlation with the total score is r= 0.93."; Sloth's summary of this work puts the main factor at 80% of the variability.<br>**A sparse item set reproduces the full scores.** | |
| 2024-09 | *Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in large language models: Indications of artificial general intelligence or achievement?*<br>@ilic2024positive | 591 LLMs on 12 Open LLM Leaderboard tests mapped to fluid reasoning, knowledge, reading/writing and quantitative ability (preprint arXiv 2310.11616, Oct 2023) | **A general factor of ability emerges from a positive manifold across 591 models.** In the preferred specification the first factor has a loading of 0.81 (R² 0.66); Ruan et al. cite it as a single factor explaining 85% of Leaderboard performance.<br>**Parameter count correlates positively with the general factor, with diminishing returns.** | ![Benchmark correlations and the preferred two-factor model, from @ilic2024positive](images/2025-10-21-15-33-31.png) |
| 2024-10 | *Danoliteracy of Generative Large Language Models*<br>@holm2025danoliteracy | Danish-language benchmark, 8 scenarios (citizenship test, social-media QA, …), open and API models incl. GPT-4 and Claude Opus | **One factor explains 95% of scenario-performance variance for Danish.** A narrow domain, but the same structure as the English-language results. | |
| 2024-10 | *Towards a Generalized Performance Benchmark for LLM Capabilities (Project MPG)*<br>@spangher2024generalized | 14 models incl. GPT-4o, o1-preview, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, Mistral Large 2, and open models; ~13 benchmarks grouped by hand into three subdomains | **A single aggregate score correlates 0.9157 (Pearson) with Chatbot Arena and 0.8326 with MMLU.**<br>**Different models lead different subdomains.** GPT-4o on factual recall, Mistral on social sensitivity, Gemini Pro on problem solving. The hierarchy is imposed by hand, not extracted from the data. | |
| 2024-12 | *Sloth: scaling laws for LLM skills to predict multi-benchmark performance across families*<br>@polo2025sloth | 30 model families (53 if base and instruct are split) on 12 benchmarks from Open LLM Leaderboard v1/v2; NeurIPS 2025 | **The best-predicting factor model has three latent skills, and they are only weakly correlated.** Reasoning, knowledge and instruction following, with skill correlations 0.12 (reasoning–knowledge), 0.43 (reasoning–IF) and 0.20 (knowledge–IF); with two skills the correlation is 0.61.<br>**The skills scale differently.** Reasoning grows with model size; knowledge with size and training tokens. | |
| 2025-02 | *Line Goes Up? Inherent Limitations of Benchmarks for Evaluating Large Language Models*<br>@fodor2025linegoesup | Argument paper, no new data | **A positive manifold across benchmarks need not indicate a general cognitive capability.** Many tasks that require intelligence in humans are solvable by systems without general competence, so benchmark aggregates are argued to be unsuitable as measures of it. | |
| 2025-03 | *General Scales Unlock AI Evaluation with Explanatory and Predictive Power*<br>@zhou2025generalscales | 15 LLMs (GPT-4o, o1, o1-mini, LLaMA 3.1/3.2 1B–405B, DeepSeek-R1 distills) on 63 tasks from 20 benchmarks, 16,108 instances | **Population-based factor solutions are unstable across model samples.** Burnell et al. found three factors and Ilić & Gignac one, months apart, on different models.<br>**Eighteen rubric-defined demand dimensions, annotated per item, predict success without any factor analysis.** GPT-4o annotations agree with a five-human consensus at rWG 0.86 on average. | |
| 2025-07 | *Train-before-Test Harmonizes Language Model Rankings*<br>@zhang2025trainbeforetest | 61 models from six families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Pythia, GPT-2, Yi) on 24 benchmarks | **Under ordinary evaluation the first principal component explains 70% of variance; after a small task-specific fine-tune of every model it explains 86%, and 93% within the Qwen family.** "train-before-test renders the score matrix essentially rank one." and "model potential is dominated by one single principal axis."<br>**Benchmark rankings agree far more after train-before-test.** Cross-benchmark Kendall's τ rises from 0.52 to 0.76.<br>**PC1 aligns with pre-training compute.** | |
| 2025-07 | *From Benchmarks to Skills: Low-Rank Factors for LLM Evaluation*<br>@maimon2025iq | 60 LLMs on 44 benchmarks, exploratory factor analysis | **Eight interpretable low-rank factors, not one, are proposed to describe the score matrix.** The strongest multi-factor solution in this literature. | ![Eight-factor profiles of two models, from @maimon2025iq](images/2025-12-05-06-36-08.png) |
| 2025-10 | *Epoch Capabilities Index*<br>@epoch2025eci; method in *A Rosetta Stone for AI Benchmarks*, @ho2025rosetta (Dec 2025) | Over three dozen benchmarks stitched into one scale | **A one-dimensional IRT model is assumed and used to place every model and benchmark on a single capability scale.** Predicted score = sigmoid(discriminability × (capability − difficulty)); the scale is then used to track progress and algorithmic efficiency over time. Unidimensionality is a modelling choice here, not a test. | |
| 2026-02 | *Quantifying construct validity in large language model evaluations*<br>@kearns2026constructvalidity | Open LLM Leaderboard results | **A model in which scale drives capabilities and capabilities drive scores fits better than a plain latent-factor model.** The "structured capabilities" model beats latent-factor models on parsimonious fit indices and beats scaling laws at predicting held-out benchmarks. | |
| 2026-03 | *A Neuropsychologically Grounded Evaluation of LLM Cognitive Abilities*<br>@haznitrama2026neurocognition | 156 models on 10 benchmarks plus three adapted neuropsychological tests (Raven's matrices, spatial working memory, Wisconsin card sorting) | **Factor analysis confirms a general factor across the benchmarks.**<br>**The same models still fail tasks trivial for humans.** Performance degrades with images and with task complexity. | |
| 2026-04 | *Growing Pains: Extensible and Efficient LLM Benchmarking Via Fixed Parameter Calibration*<br>@habba2026growingpains | More than 400 models; multidimensional IRT with anchor items | **Between three and eight interpretable skill dimensions explain much of the variance.**<br>**One hundred anchor questions per dataset predict full-evaluation scores within 2–3 percentage points.** | |
| 2026-07 | *CogArena: A Multimethod Evaluation of Cognitive Ability Structure in Large Language Models*<br>@hou2026cogarena | 55 open-weight models on 13 cognitive paradigms in 5 groupings (working memory, cognitive control, episodic memory, theory of mind, metacognition) | **Nearly all paradigm correlations are positive and a common axis explains about half the variance.**<br>**The within-grouping advantage is small and sensitive to scoring.** | |

### Gaps

- Almost all factor analyses use open-weight models on the Open LLM Leaderboard family of benchmarks. Frontier proprietary and reasoning models appear only in small samples (14 in Spangher et al., 15 in Zhou et al., an appendix in Ruan et al.), so whether o1-class models break the manifold (math and code up, knowledge flat) has not been measured.
- No study includes agentic, long-horizon or computer-use benchmarks in the score matrix; the manifold is established on short-answer tasks.
- The number of factors is sample-dependent (three in Burnell et al., one in Ilić & Gignac, three in Sloth, eight in Maimon et al.) and no study has tested whether the first factor extracted on one model population predicts a benchmark introduced after those models were trained.
- Nothing compares the LLM factor structure with the human factor structure on the same items; the question the chapter raises about a shared axis remains open.
- The strongest single-factor result (Zhang et al., 86–93%) holds only after equalising task-specific preparation; under ordinary evaluation the same data give 70%.
